title: After the 10,000-worker factory vanished, he had 20 years of snapshots of migrant life
dek: Others photographed the era's anomalies; he insisted on its ordinary days — meals, punch-ins, English classes. When the giant factory finally disappeared, almost no one else had kept the archive.
why: Not an industry analysis — a migrant worker using a camera to write a biography of himself and his generation. The back half, on ‘density’ and ‘autoethnography’, is the most valuable part.
who: Founders and content people interested in the shift in manufacturing, documentary photography, and the situation of migrant workers; anyone who wants to understand how the Pearl River Delta factory era disappeared.
skip: The show promo and event notices at the start, 0:00-1:08, can be skipped.

points.h: The logic of the assembly line is to make a person's value irrelevant
points.body: After the Foxconn suicides, Zhan Youbing was asked what he thought. He said he had seriously considered it: every assembly-line method works by subdividing the process so that manufacturing is more stable and people are more replaceable. Translated, those two sentences mean — anyone can do it, and anyone will do it just as well. The machines had not yet replaced the workers, but the person's value already barely mattered. That was the underlying motive for him later picking up a camera and aiming it at his fellow workers: inside a system deliberately flattening individual difference, to record specific people.

points.h: Riding the green-skin train felt like climbing into a bandits' den
points.body: In 1995, after leaving the army, he went south. The car was already full at the Wuchang origin station — people above the seats, people below, people sleeping on the luggage racks, people everywhere in the toilets and the gangways between cars. At Chenzhou someone smashed a window with a brick and shoved people onto the train like livestock. For more than thirty hours he could not sit and could not drink water; after getting off, his belly was badly swollen. At Guangzhou railway station he was then cheated by touts into being ‘sold like a piglet’ — first they took twenty-odd yuan saying it was for Dongguan, then on the highway they demanded another ten for the expressway toll, and if you refused someone would come up and slap you, and in the end you were dumped in a wasteland with no village ahead and no shop behind to change vehicles. He says he used the term for years before he understood what it meant last year.

points.h: He did 102 push-ups for a security guard job
points.body: In 1995 it was hard to find work; men had a far harder time than women, and factory recruitment notices stated outright that they only hired female workers aged 18 to 25. He saw a hiring notice by National Highway 107, and the security captain had all the applicants lie down in the parking lot and do push-ups to screen their stamina. The count was drawn out; by 20 people began dropping, by 40 only eight or ten were left, by 50-something only he was left. The captain said you're bragging, go ahead, and he did 102. Then he was told to spar with someone; the other man did a split, and he turned sideways, caught the leg and flipped him. That was how he got his first job: gate security at a hotel, 450 yuan a month.

points.h: An 1,800-yuan camera and 48-yuan rolls of film
points.body: In 2002 he agonised for a long time before buying his own camera: his wage was only around 1,500, he already had a child, and his wife was still back home. He called to discuss it, and his wife said, if you like it, buy it. The camera was 1,800 yuan; film, even bought ten rolls at a time wholesale, was 48 each, plus 5 for developing and another ten or twenty for prints — a huge drain on him in that era. At first he shot factory events, visiting guests, employee tug-of-war, assuming that photography was just a technical problem of getting things sharp. Later, reading Chinese photography magazines, he found there was so much learning in photography and he had no standard to measure by, so he bought the New York Institute of Photography textbook, whose first lesson is the three criteria of a good photograph.

points.h: A model-contest photo passed ten million clicks, then he was told to delete it
points.body: In 2007 the factory began holding a model contest; the women went on stage in swimsuits, evening gowns and uniforms, and there was pole dancing. In 2008 he changed position, went to the stage backdrop and shot downward — models in front, a dense black mass of audience behind — and sent it to Tencent in time; it went up on the portal and got tens of millions of clicks in a morning. But online comments said this was picking a mistress for the boss and a lover for the factory manager; the framing was distorted, the boss came under enormous pressure, and he was told to delete it. Tencent said it could only be hidden, other sites' viral reposting could not be stopped, and in the end he was served a notice reserving the right to pursue the matter.

points.h: The photo of the woman worker looking up — he had not planned to use it
points.body: On 5 January 2011, as a senior supervisor, he entered the clean room to inspect fire safety, and because the work required it he openly brought his camera. Clean-room work allows a four-minute break after two hours; the changing area was hung with unworn clean-room suits, and two people sat in front, one of them a fellow Hubei native. He pressed the shutter once or twice, and his fellow townsman heard the sound and looked up at him. He says the advice he was given when learning photography was that ‘a photo where the subject looks at the lens is not a good photo’, so he never used this one. Later Ren Yue, a teacher at Renmin University of China, organised the Off-Pix award; he submitted it, and it was unexpectedly made the lead image. Looking at it seriously afterwards, he admitted it has its own pull — different readers will have different inner responses, so a photographer should interpret his own photos as little as possible.

points.h: One set of ID papers lent to many people; after social security went online, his years of service were zeroed out
points.body: When he came out to find work in 1995, Hubei people were not wanted, Henan people were not wanted, Anhui people were acceptable, so he borrowed an Anhui man's ID card. At the time factories' information was separate, there was no networked computer system, and the social security system did not require contributions, so that set of papers was lent to many people and entered many factories. But after 2000 social security began to be networked, and the system would not accept it — same ID number, same name, same household registration address — and the enterprises decided you were dishonest and zeroed out your years of service. He says this won't do: our generation is about to reach retirement age, and those years of service are real. When even present-day life has no security, it is impossible to think about retirement twenty or fifty years away.

points.h: Density: he shot for 20 years before discovering it was everywhere
points.body: In 2019 he curated a set of photographs around the density of migrant working life, which won the Excellence Award and the Alpa Award at the third Hard Instant Image Awards. Workers' gatherings shot from high above, heads packed with almost no gaps; collective dormitories hung with clothes, from a distance airtight; workshop switches, key cabinets, lockers holding bowls and chopsticks — neatly divided structures producing a visual sense of density. He says at first it was unconscious: shooting with his phone every day, shooting security training, shooting any fellow worker he happened to see on the road, accumulating day by day, on and off for almost 20 years. When there were so many eras in so many factories, he had not observed in that way, and once he discovered it, it was terrifying — even the switches looked spectacular.

points.h: Time as the warp, space as the weft: a lifetime to understand one society
points.body: The full thread he worked out is: time as the warp, space as the weft, the life cycle as the outline, capital's impact on the industrial zone as the axis, forming a comprehensive three-dimensional record including sound, images, video, text and objects. Later he changed methods: starting from the keyword dagong, he found ten main keywords on Baidu Scholar, then searched all related terms on Baidu, got 322, went into Baidu Images and began screenshotting them all — this is the internet's understanding of dagong, to be presented together with his own photographic understanding in one huge exhibition space. He says this is us watching the era from inside an illusory era, while the real era is ignored. He compares himself to a Sherpa: the famous mountaineers get the credit, but it is the Sherpas who carry the loads — I'll just be that Sherpa.

terms.def: In the mid-Qing, Cantonese were shipped to America to build railways like piglets being transported; later it meant being cheated by middlemen and drivers who piled on charges along the way to work.
The researcher takes himself as the object of study, recording the life of the group he belongs to rather than studying an outside ethnic group.
Magnum, the internationally known photography agency; Zhan Youbing studied the work of its photographers one by one on its website.
A photography award organised by Ren Yue, a teacher at Renmin University of China; Zhan Youbing submitted to it and was shown as the lead image.

quotes.text: Back then when you came out to work, it wasn't about riding a train — you felt like you'd climbed into a bandits' den.
This is the era: we watch the era from inside an illusory era, while the real era is ignored.
I often say that if we use a lifetime to understand a society, the understanding we arrive at will certainly not be poor; but if we can see a society in a single day, it will certainly be shallow.
